extracted.intended_audience: researchers, clinicians, managers, policymakers, and designers implementing or evaluating technology-supported health and social care programs
extracted.subtask_description: Using the NASSS framework to predict, evaluate, design, implement, scale up, or explain failure of technology-supported health or social care programs by examining multiple interacting domains and their dynamics over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: The condition or illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about the clinical condition/problem for which the technology is intended (its nature, prognosis, heterogeneity, multimorbidity, need for customization, and whether it is simple, complicated, or complex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the condition is textbook/simple or heterogeneous and unpredictable; consider multimorbidity and the need for customization (eg, many patients require ongoing adaptation of care packages). The framework notes a key limitation of prior frameworks was failing to analyse the condition in detail; start with a realistic assessment of the nature and likely progression of the condition and focus on what matters to the user (ARCHIE principle: anchored, realistic).

rubrics_metrics.name: The technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Material properties, functionality, interoperability, usability, aesthetic properties, and symbolic properties of the technology (what it does, how it looks/feels, and what it signifies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate physical features, functionality, interoperability, dependability, and usability; consider symbolic meanings (eg, mobile phones symbolize youth/progress; GPS/pendant alarms may symbolize dependence). Distinguish types of technology (eg, remote monitoring that transmits objective biomarkers vs remote communication enabling conversations). Antipatterns include ignoring symbolic properties, assuming off-the-shelf tech needs no customization, or neglecting ongoing support and tinkering needed in real-world use.

rubrics_metrics.name: The value proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technology is likely to be worth introducing—its perceived benefits and costs to different stakeholders, and the alignment (or misalignment) between supply-side and demand-side value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider upstream value (investors, business case, regulators) and downstream value (clinicians, policy makers, patients). Evaluate trade-offs for patients between benefits, costs, work required to use technology, and concerns about medicalization/surveillance. Check for poor alignment between commercial/business incentives and clinical/user needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: The adopter system (professional staff, patient, and lay caregivers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The people (staff, patients, lay caregivers) who must adopt and use the technology and the social and professional processes that shape their uptake and ongoing use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine factors influencing staff acceptance (professional identity, norms, perceived usefulness/ease of use), patient engagement, and the role of lay caregivers; use models such as technology acceptance and social learning but also sociological accounts (eg, normalization process theory). Pay attention to recruitment/engagement approach, training/support needs, and local champions. Antipatterns: assuming individual uptake without considering team/relational dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: The organization(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational capacity, routines, governance, resources, business processes, procurement arrangements, and readiness to implement and sustain the technology-supported program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess absorptive capacity, existing routines, potential for workarounds, leadership and managerial support, funding lines, business models, and whether the organization can provide ongoing support/training. Look for presence/absence of local champions, and note that organizations may vary widely in engagement. Examples show variable staff engagement and need for organizational workarounds to make services function.

rubrics_metrics.name: The wider (institutional and societal) context
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory, legal, policy, socio-cultural, economic, and infrastructural context (eg, broadband availability, inequalities) that shapes adoption, scale-up, spread, and sustainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider national/local policy, regulation, cross-border legal issues, socio-economic determinants (age, sex, SES, ethnicity), digital divide and infrastructure constraints. The paper highlights that social determinants pattern conditions and access (eg, poorer groups have less broadband/digital literacy), and that policy enthusiasm may be insufficient without contextual fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: The interaction and mutual adaptation between all these domains over time
rubrics_metrics.description: The dynamic, recursive relationships and adaptations among condition, technology, adopters, organizations, and context as the program evolves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how domains co-evolve, require tinkering and customization, and produce emergent behaviours; use longitudinal, interdisciplinary, naturalistic methods to capture these dynamics. The framework cautions that complexity across multiple domains makes mainstreaming unlikely; prospective and retrospective application of NASSS can reveal adaptation needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity classification of domains (simple / complicated / complex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each NASSS domain should be classified as simple (straightforward, predictable, few components), complicated (multiple interacting components/issues), or complex (dynamic, unpredictable, not easily disaggregated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to predict implementation difficulty: programs with complicated domains can be difficult but feasible; programs with complexity in multiple domains rarely become mainstreamed. Apply the classification prospectively to identify risk of nonadoption or abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of knowledge generated by the technology (cold vs warm telehealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technology primarily transmits objective biomarkers/structured data ('cold' telehealth) or enables conversational, relational interactions ('warm' telehealth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that different knowledge types change what is included/excluded in care (eg, biomarker feeds vs rich clinician-patient conversations). Design, evaluation, and workforce implications differ by type of knowledge the tech produces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value proposition: upstream versus downstream considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish value as seen by investors/regulators/business (upstream) from value as seen by clinicians, policymakers, and patients (downstream).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess evidence of efficacy/safety and auditable business processes for upstream actors, while evaluating patient outcomes, costs, and service impact for downstream actors. Watch for misalignment between these perspectives that can undermine adoption or sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient engagement influences (digital health engagement model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four key influences on whether an individual will engage with a health technology: personal agency and motivation, personal life and values, the engagement/recruitment approach used, and the quality of the health technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning implementation, assess patient capacity and motivation (including illness burden), tailor recruitment/engagement methods, and ensure technology quality/usability. Antipatterns: assuming mass dissemination without active recruitment/support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinician resistance model (four elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A model identifying four elements of clinician resistance to new health care technology: resistance to the policy reflected in the technology; resistance to sociomaterial constraints (eg, clunkiness); resistance to compromised professional practice; and resistance to compromised professional relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to diagnose staff objections and design mitigations (eg, address professional concerns about scope of practice, provide reliable technology, engage clinicians in design). Recognize professional acceptance may be the single most important determinant of local success.

rubrics_metrics.name: ARCHIE principles for design/evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and evaluation principles for assisted living/health technologies: anchored, realistic, cocreative, human, integrated, and evaluated (ARCHIE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with an anchored, realistic assessment of needs; co-create with users; ensure human-centred and integrated design; and build in evaluation. Antipattern: designing without codesign, training, or realistic user assessment (as with Product A example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequalities in access, uptake, and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of how age, sex, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, social networks, housing, debt, and digital literacy shape differential access to and use of technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly assess equity impacts and the digital divide (eg, broadband availability), since disadvantaged groups often have greater need but less access; include strategies to mitigate inequities in design and implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of whether the technology is 'worth introducing'
rubrics_metrics.description: A pragmatic appraisal of likely net benefit considering benefits, costs, required user work, user capacity, and acceptability of surveillance/medicalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate trade-offs from multiple stakeholder perspectives; perform realistic business-case and downstream-impact appraisal before large-scale introduction. Antipattern: introducing technology driven by policy enthusiasm or commercial pressure without evidence of downstream value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for training, recruitment, and ongoing support / business model alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess requirements for user training, active recruitment strategies, helpdesk/support, and sustainable business models (eg, who pays, who provides help).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Product A vs Product B cases illustrate that lack of training/support and absence of a viable dissemination/support model leads to failure. Plan for mass awareness, active invitation, pilot selection, and helpdesk or support services where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence and role of local champions and normalization processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of influential local champions who can persuade peers and help normalize the technology-supported service within professional groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and support champions to encourage uptake; use normalization process theory constructs (eg, relational integration) to assess whether the technology fits professional norms. Antipattern: expecting passive diffusion without champions or visible peer adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material affordances, customization, and need for tinkering
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the technology and its service require onsite tinkering, customization, liaison with suppliers, and adaptation of work routines to be acceptable and safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan resources and processes for ongoing customization and problem-solving (eg, device configuration, supplier liaison, workflow adjustment). The empirical cases show high degrees of tinkering were often needed to reach acceptable solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate evaluation methods for complex sociotechnical programs
rubrics_metrics.description: The framework recommends interdisciplinary, nondeterministic, locally situated, longitudinal, qualitative and mixed-methods approaches rather than relying solely on randomized controlled trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hermeneutic review, ethnography, action research, and naturalistic methods to capture dynamic interactions and emergent phenomena; RCTs alone may miss sociotechnical interactions that explain nonadoption or abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of symbolic properties and stigma
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the technology's symbolic meanings for users (eg, stigma, connotations of dependence or progress) that may affect acceptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include exploration of how users perceive the technology socially and culturally; symbolic negatives can reduce uptake even if functionality is adequate.
